q-11884:
The standard equation of an upward- or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

To write the given equation in this form, we need to group the $x$-terms on the left-hand side and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-30x-8y+67 & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-30x & =8y-67 \\ 3[{x}^{2}-10x] & =8y-67 \\ 3[(x-5)^{2}-25] & =8y-67 \\ 3(x-5)^{2}-75 & =8y-67 \\ 3(x-5)^{2} & =8y-67+75 \\ 3(x-5)^{2} & =8y+8 \\ 3(x-5)^{2} & =8(y+1) \\ (x-5)^{2} & =\frac{8}{3}(y+1) \\ (x-5)^{2} & =4(\frac{2}{3})(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k)=(5,-1).$

q-103668:
The standard equation of an upward- or downward-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(x-h)^{2}=4p(y-k),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

To write the given equation in this form, we need to group the $x$-terms on the left-hand side and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x-2y-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+2x & =2y+1 \\ (x+1)^{2}-1 & =2y+1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =2y+1+1 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =2y+2 \\ (x+1)^{2} & =4(\frac{1}{2})(y+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k)=(-1,-1).$

q-86523:
The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

To write the given equation in this form, we need to group the $y$-terms on the left-hand side and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}-2x+18y+29 & =0 \\ 3{y}^{2}+18y & =2x-29 \\ 3[{y}^{2}+6y] & =2x-29 \\ 3[(y+3)^{2}-9] & =2x-29 \\ 3(y+3)^{2}-27 & =2x-29 \\ 3(y+3)^{2} & =2x-29+27 \\ 3(y+3)^{2} & =2x-2 \\ 3(y+3)^{2} & =2(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{2}{3}(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{1}{6})(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k)=(1,-3).$

q-103680:
The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ is

$$
(y-k)^{2}=4p(x-h),
$$

where $p$ is constant.

To write the given equation in this form, we need to group the $y$-terms on the left-hand side and complete the square, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4x-4y+24 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =4x-24 \\ (y-2)^{2}-4 & =4x-24 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4x-24+4 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4x-20 \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4(x-5) \\ (y-2)^{2} & =4(1)(x-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the vertex are $(h,k)=(5,2).$

q-84082:
The standard equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
a=\sqrt{64}=8,\,b=\sqrt{4}=2.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\pm \frac{8}{2}x \\  & =\pm 4x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-116564:
The standard equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{y}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a vertical hyperbola centered at the origin, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y=\pm \frac{a}{b}x.
$$

To rewrite the given equation in standard form, we divide both sides of the equation by $200$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}^{2}-25{x}^{2} & =200 \\ \frac{8{y}^{2}}{200}-\frac{25{x}^{2}}{200} & =\frac{200}{200} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{25}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $a=\sqrt{25}=5,$ and $b=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are $y=\pm \frac{5}{2\sqrt{2}}x=\pm \frac{5\sqrt{2}}{4}x.$

q-8461:
The rotation matrix ${R}_{\theta }$ represents a rotation of angle $\theta $ counterclockwise about the origin and is given by

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & -\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}],
$$

Comparing $A$ with the rotation matrix, we have 

$$
{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{2} \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta >0$ and $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta <0$ we must have $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi .$ 

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$

The principal value $\theta $ is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}})=-\frac{\pi }{6},
$$

Therefore, $A$ represents a rotation of $\frac{\pi }{6}$ radians *clockwise* about the origin.

q-17330:
For expressions involving subtraction, De Moivre's theorem states that

$$
{[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\phi )-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\phi )]}^{n}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\phi )-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\phi ).
$$

In our expression, we have $n=16$ and $\phi =\frac{\theta }{2}.$ Substituting in these values, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})]}^{16} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(16\cdot \frac{\theta }{2})-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(16\cdot \frac{\theta }{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\theta )-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-81769:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (1-2t)\text{d}t \\  & =t-{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(4)=-6.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =(4)-(4)^{2}+C \\ -6 & =4-16+C \\ -6 & =-12+C \\ C & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=-{t}^{2}+t+6.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *right*, we must solve the inequality $v>0.$ This gives

$$
-{t}^{2}+t+6=-({t}^{2}-t-6)=-(t+2)(t-3)>0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t),$ we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/74db16dc00f5d08637cef02960409b7fd15c4bd3c19f577fa5a1f30ac8c402d3.png)

From the graph, we see that $v>0$ whenever $0<t<3.$

q-120757:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (3{t}^{2}-6t-4)\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=0.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =(4)^{3}-3(4)^{2}-4(4)+C \\ C & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t.$

To find the time interval in which the particle is moving to the *left*, we must solve the inequality $v<0.$ This gives

$$
{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}-4t=t(t-4)(t+1)<0.
$$

Plotting the graph of $v(t)$, we get the following picture.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14063912/assets/002f547b882940d087d6ed9d228334ec163931cfea0665eafdfe8b6ec8d863da.png)

From the graph, we see that $v<0$ whenever $0<t<4.$

q-120784:
The extrema of the velocity $v$ occur at the critical points of $v.$

Since $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=a(t),$ to find the times where $v$ is a maximum, we just need to solve $a(t)=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $a(t)=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =0 \\ 15-3t & =0 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

We now test the extreme value using the second derivative test. For this, we find the second derivative of $v(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}v}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(15-3t) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${v}^{″}(5)<0,$ we conclude that the velocity is maximized when $t=5\,\text{s}.$

Now, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (15-3t)\text{d}t \\  & =15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(1)=14.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}15(1)-\frac{3}{2}(1)^{2}+C & =14 \\ C & =\frac{3}{2}-1\,⟹\,C=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{1}{2}+15t-\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}.$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{\text{max}}=v(5)=\frac{1}{2}+15(5)-\frac{3}{2}(5)^{2}=38\,\text{m}/\text{s}
$$

q-85609:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3+{t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{2-t},\,4{t}^{3}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{2-t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{2-t},\,12{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the acceleration at time $t=2,$ we substitute $t=2$ into the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}a(2) & =⟨{e}^{2-2},12(2)^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,48⟩\end{aligned}
$$

q-121931:
To compute the acceleration vector, we need to differentiate the velocity vector. So first, we need to compute the velocity vector, which we can do this by differentiating the position vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t-{t}^{3}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}+t)⟩ \\  & =⟨4-3{t}^{2},4t+1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute the acceleration vector, we differentiate the velocity vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t},\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-3{t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-6t,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

q-75278:
The normal is horizontal if the tangent is vertical. Therefore, we require ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${y}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

So, we first find the derivatives of $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-8\operatorname{sin}⁡4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=12\operatorname{cos}⁡4t.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving ${x}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
-8\operatorname{sin}⁡4t=0\,⟹\,t=0,\frac{\pi }{4}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(0) & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=12\ne 0, \\ {y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )=-12\ne 0,\end{aligned}
$$

which confirms that the normal to the curve is indeed horizontal when $t=0$ and $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$

q-122931:
First, we find the coordinates of the point $C$ by substituting $t=1$ into the parametric equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =e, \\ y & =2(1){e}^{1}-2{e}^{1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So we're looking to find the equation of the tangent line to the curve at the point $(e,0).$  For this, we need to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ which means we first need to find the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ as follows:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={e}^{t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=2t{e}^{t}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)} \\  & =\frac{2t{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =2t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point where $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{dy}{dx}|}_{t=1} & =2(1)=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope ${m}_{n}$ of the normal line, we take the negative reciprocal of $m$:

$$
{m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\,2\,}
$$

To calculate the equation of the normal, we use point-slope form with the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(e,0)$ and the slope ${m}_{n}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =(-\frac{1}{2})(x-e) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{e}{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$
